sentences.text: Canada's distinctive role in the Allied Industrial Base is as a resource and processing anchor: it ranks first among allies on resource & processing positions, and 19 economies count it as their best-placed trusted partner somewhere in the chain.
That role is allied before it is national: at home, uranium mining reads Watch, and battery and EV mineral mining, where Canada holds only 1% of world supply, read Partner.
Its industrial effort should go into batteries, where it makes cells and packs, has committed investment in components and holds a supplier role in nickel chemicals.
The fence that matters is narrow: the rare-earth chain, to be secured with allied partners.
Only gas networks need faster deployment, and recorded protection should shift away from steps the strategy leaves open.
The rare-earth chain from refining to traction magnets, where China holds 94% of world supply and trusted suppliers only 4% (shares that battery materials refining repeats).
The answer is qualified trusted supply built with allies, stocks until it qualifies and phased limits on adversary sources, not self-sufficiency.

Catch Up in battery components, on committed investment, and in battery materials refining, on its export share of refined battery materials; build EV manufacturing on committed investment and extend gas-turbine equipment.
Keep uranium, nickel chemicals and aluminium wire rod reliable for allies, and above all nuclear special materials: an allied commitment, not a domestic fence.

Battery and EV minerals from trusted producers such as Australia and the United States, where the allied model finds supply covers the need; coal-plant equipment from allied makers; solar-grade polysilicon.
With developing partners, add trusted battery capacity through development finance and offtake.
Accelerate gas networks, buying equipment competitively from trusted suppliers, and build storage, grid, wind and solar on a market footing.
Leave open wafers and PV cells, grid metals refining and grid components, and gas liquids processing.
In Figure 1, Partner sits in battery and EV minerals and coal-plant hardware, and Catch Up fills most manufacturing columns, including the nuclear chain after mining.
The orange corner flag marks the traction magnets, the only High-fence part inside another step; grey flags mark Watch layers, such as control software, inside Catch Up steps.
Each cell is a supply-chain step of a technology, colored by its strategic choice.
A corner flag marks a mixed step whose named parts sit behind a different fence: in EV drivetrain components, the traction magnets are Secure and the step Catch Up.
A dotted outline marks a review case, a call resting on low confidence, a review flag, a thin anchor or a known data artifact; this brief does not turn those calls into recommendations.

Secure is a narrow call for Canada: one whole step and one layer inside another step, which form one capability.
The rare-earth chain: separation, metals and magnets
Feeds the traction magnets of EV motors.
The refining step also covers battery metals; Canada holds 1% of its world supply and <1% of world exports.
China holds 94% of world supply and trusted suppliers 4%; it provides 37% of Canada's imports, and rebuilding takes more than three years.
New trusted separation, metal and magnet capacity with allies such as Japan, Australia and the United States, through co-investment and offtake, and at home where a foothold can be built.
Stocks until it qualifies; adversary-source limits in critical uses, phased in.
The magnets of blades, towers and nacelle parts read Catch Up there but Secure in EV drivetrains; this brief treats both as the same chain.
No control software sits behind the fence: grid, inverter, turbine and vehicle control layers read Watch.
The hardware shares are modest (for example, 22% of PV module and inverter imports), and the data do not measure who supplies the software.
Medium fence — where industrial capability matters
Here Canada makes its real industrial choices: is a capability worth having (Strategic Industrial Value), and how strong is Canada today (Competitive Position)?
Most of its 15 Catch Up steps rest on small shares of world supply in mixed trade codes, so this brief builds on few.
Battery cells and packs is the only Preserve call that clears the evidence bar: a top-quarter position (87) on operating capacity, with high value and need.
With 1% of world supply, keeping the position means expanding it.
Oil production also reads Preserve but is flagged for review by the engine, a review case, although 14 economies have Canada as their best-placed trusted partner for it.
Battery components rests on three anchors, including committed investment, with a position of 66 and high need (71); China provides 76% of Canada's imports.
Battery materials refining has high confidence but a single anchor, 6% of world exports, and a position of 0: a trade position to build from, not proven refining capacity.
The AIB's share of nickel intermediates and chemicals (10%) corroborates the nickel side, not lithium, cathode or anode materials.
EV and charger manufacturing adds committed investment to small trade shares, from a low position (5).
Gas turbines and LNG plant (47) and gas-turbine and drilling components (30) extend existing positions with high confidence.
In transformers, switchgear and cables, whose value just clears the bar, the case sits in large power transformers, power conversion and HVDC control.
EV drivetrain components starts from almost no position (1), so it is a build with allied partners.
Other Catch Up calls are weaker than they look, and this brief does not build on them:
Uranium conversion and enrichment: a supply share (3%) that more likely reflects uranium compounds, concentrate included, than conversion capacity; the enrichment layers inherit it.
Reactors, nuclear fuel and reactor parts: baskets that mix reactor and fuel lines with generic boiler and steam-turbine parts.
Wind turbines and their parts: positions of 7 and 17 in trade codes dominated by cables, transformers and switchgear, with towers that include transmission masts.
PV modules and inverters: moderate confidence, Watch modules, and trade codes that include chip-making machines.
Battery recycling: an export share (19%) of battery waste, scrap and residues.
Drilling rigs, tankers and oil equipment: a value at the bar (60) and moderate confidence.
Battery and EV mineral mining have very high need (96), but their value is capped below the bar because it rests on market size alone.
Source them deliberately from trusted producers such as Australia and the United States; allied supply covers the need.
Coal-plant hardware reads Partner on high need and low value: diversified contracts with allied makers such as Japan, Germany and Italy should suffice, on weak partner evidence.
Solar-grade polysilicon is a Partner layer, and rare-earth and wind materials refining reads Partner on low confidence, a review case.
